At the very outset, it may be noted that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts, as are required in a criminal prosecution.
The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the M.V. Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
6 9 . At the very outset, it may be noted that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts, as are required in a criminal prosecution.
The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the M.V. Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.
Reference in this regard can be made to the prepositions of MACT No. 466/19 Kavita Devi & Ors. Vs. Bijender Singh & Ors.
Pages No. 9/29 LOVLEEN 2023.04.21 law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi and others Vs.
Himachal Road Transport Corporation and others, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs. Amir Chand and others 2011 (1) SCR 1096(Civil Appeal No.1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs.
Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303 etc.
10.
A bare perusal of cross examination of PW-2 reveals that he (PW-2) did not see the collision which happened between the TSR and the rear portion of the offending vehicle.
The effect of oral testimony of PW-2 is that the collision between the TSR and the offending vehicle was simultaneous with the collision of his car and the offending vehicle.
But, as per R1/R3W1, the collision between the TSR and the offending vehicle took place after a little hiatus ( i.e. after the offending vehicle had already been brought to a halt by R1/R3W1).
Accordingly, the defence raised by R1/R3W1, to the effect that the collision between the TSR and the rear portion of the offending vehicle took place after the offending vehicle had been brought to a halt by R1/R3W1, is hereby rejected.
In the facts and circumstances, it could be safely held that the collision between the TSR and the offending vehicle took place simultaneously with the collision between the offending vehicle and the car of PW-2.
15.
Having observed so, it could be safely inferred that at the relevant time R1/R3W1 applied sudden brakes to the offending vehicle just MACT No. 466/19 Kavita Devi & Ors.
Vs. Bijender Singh & Ors.
